guitars.note: Brand-new listing (created 2026-08-01). Priced ~$1.5-2k under typical used R9 VOS market - strong deal if legit; OHSC + COA + case candy included. Established shop. Ask for serial and in-hand weight confirmation.
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

Known issues: few model-specific faults — the usual Custom Shop lottery (nut work, occasional heavy examples, VOS finish inconsistency); some V3 buyers report neck-profile surprise; anniversary-specific parts fade unevenly on played examples.

Market/value: reasonably collectible one-year anniversary run with hand-selected specs; sells used around or slightly above standard R0 money; clean V2 examples resell more easily than V3 (very slim neck narrows the buyer pool).

Verify before buying: which neck version it actually is (get caliper measurements — V2/V3 mislabeling is common on Reverb), COA/anniversary paperwork, weight, anniversary-correct knobs/plastics, and unmodified unpotted pickups.

research: Neck feel: 2015-16 True Historic R0s use the re-scanned 'True Historic' 1960 carve — slim but shouldered, roughly .82-.85" at the 1st fret, with more accurate contours than 2013-14 models; described as the most vintage-accurate slim neck of its era.
Pickups: True Historic-spec unpotted Custombuckers — sweet, open and dynamic; tonally the same league as current Custombuckers.

Known issues: MLP consensus is 2015 batches were excellent but wood/top selection slipped in 2016; double-carved tops and thin-skin lacquer check easily; correct-material TH plastics shrink and crack like the originals; 'costs 30% more for 10% better' complaints dominate period threads.

Market/value: strong collector reputation as a short-lived top-of-line run — THs resell above standard 2013-16 Historics; R0 versions are rarer than R9s and considered sleepers; beware ordinary Historics passed off as THs at TH prices.

Verify before buying: authentic TH identity (period-correct vintage-style serial starting 0 xxxx, TH-specific COA and case), finish checking/repairs under the thin lacquer, original TH plastics, and pot/solder originality.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

research: Neck feel: these are not interchangeable — late-70s Greco EGs (Fujigen) typically run slim-to-medium with low comfortable setups ('plays better than Gibsons of that era' is a recurring tech comment), Tokai Love Rock LS models track 50s Gibson profiles with LS-number-dependent chunk, and Burny Super Grades are known on tokaiforum/mylespaul for deliberately fat 50s-style necks; always play or get profile measurements, model number alone doesn't tell you.

Pickups are the usual weak point and the usual swap: 70s Grecos shipped Maxon-made units (U-1000/U-2000, later the PAF-like Dry Z which is excellent and collectible), Tokai's better LS models carry respectable PAF-clones while budget LS ships duller units, Burny's VH-1 is widely considered one of the best stock PAF copies in any copy guitar; forum consensus is a pickup swap on a lower-tier model is normal and not value-destroying, but missing original Dry Z or VH-1 pickups should lower the price.

Known issues/tiering: quality tracks the original model number, not the brand — a Greco EG-500 or low LS/RLG is a plywood-or-veneer budget guitar while EG-1000/Super Real, LS-80+ and RLG-90+ are genuinely excellent; also verify country of origin since later Burny RLGs were made in Korea (much cheaper build), and early-70s Grecos can be bolt-neck with cheap hardware despite 'lawsuit era' branding.

Market/value: prices have climbed hard as 'lawsuit/MIJ' became a marketing word — good late-70s Greco EGs and 80s Tokai LS run roughly $1k–2.5k+ with top Super Real/Reborn examples higher, but forum threads (thefretboard, mylespaul) warn many NYC/online listings are 'severely overpriced' mid-tier guitars wearing lawsuit hype; the label 'lawsuit' technically applies only to pre-1978 open-book headstocks, so discount accordingly.

Verify before buying: decode the model tier and date (Greco serials/neck-pocket stamps and headstock logo style, Tokai serial + 'Love Rock' logo appears late-1980 onward, Burny serial or lack thereof — many legit early ones have no serial), check for the classic frankenguitar/parts-swap signs (mismatched pot codes, re-drilled tuner holes, replaced fingerboards), and beware Chinese counterfeits and re-decaled bodies now wearing Greco/Tokai/Burny or even Gibson logos — tokaiforum's ID threads ('Definitive Guide to Greco, Burny, Orville') are the reference for authentication.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

Market/value: cheapest vintage 335 window along with the early 80s — treated as gigging vintage rather than collectible; original-tarback examples have a small cult following that supports value.
Verify before buying: weight on a scale, original tarbacks (check DCR), coil-tap switch function and un-butchered wiring, neck angle/top sinking, volute-area crack repairs, finish originality.

research: Neck feel: specs say '3-piece maple neck, volute' but the range in the wild is huge — early-70s Deluxes/Customs often have slim, almost flat-shouldered necks with the small 'fretless wonder' frets on Customs (fast but hard to bend on), while late-70s/early-80s necks fill out; per mylespaul.com threads the volute is a cosmetic gripe more than a playability one, and the 3-piece maple neck is actually more break-resistant than a 1-piece mahogany Gibson neck.

Pickups: Deluxes carry Gibson mini-humbuckers — lower output, clearer and snappier than full-size 'buckers, praised in forums for cutting through a mix Tele-style; many Deluxes were routed out in the 70s/80s for full-size humbuckers (kills collector value), while Standards/Customs of the era use T-tops, now respected PAF-adjacent pickups worth real money on their own.

Known issues: weight is the big one — pancake (multi-ply) bodies 1969–77 plus maple can push Customs past 10.5–11 lbs, and weight varies wildly guitar to guitar; also watch for headstock-tip wood separation and binding chips on Customs, pancake/neck-lamination line cosmetics, and shrinking/crumbling plastics — forum consensus (e.g. mylespaul 'Pancake bodies good, bad or indifferent') is the 'Norlin era sucks' narrative is overblown, with good and bad examples every year.

Market/value: Norlins are the fastest-appreciating Gibson segment — mylespaul's 'Norlin Prices Climbing' thread and Reverb data show stock 70s Deluxes around $3.5k–4.5k and clean examples to ~$8k, Standards and Customs similar or higher, with rare finishes (cherry, sparkle, wine red) commanding premiums; 70s is 'the new vintage' as 50s/60s bursts priced everyone out.

Verify before buying: 1970–75 six-digit serials are nearly random — date via pot codes (137YYWW), 'Made in USA' stamp, volute and pancake construction details (see mylespaul FAQ 'Norlin identification 1970-1975'); check under UV/close light for headstock repairs (common, fine on a player at a discount but should knock 30-40% off), confirm mini-humbucker routes on a Deluxe are unmolested, weigh the guitar, and confirm original T-tops/mini-hums are present since pickup swaps are rampant.

research: Neck feel: these are not interchangeable — late-70s Greco EGs (Fujigen) typically run slim-to-medium with low comfortable setups ('plays better than Gibsons of that era' is a recurring tech comment), Tokai Love Rock LS models track 50s Gibson profiles with LS-number-dependent chunk, and Burny Super Grades are known on tokaiforum/mylespaul for deliberately fat 50s-style necks; always play or get profile measurements, model number alone doesn't tell you.

Pickups are the usual weak point and the usual swap: 70s Grecos shipped Maxon-made units (U-1000/U-2000, later the PAF-like Dry Z which is excellent and collectible), Tokai's better LS models carry respectable PAF-clones while budget LS ships duller units, Burny's VH-1 is widely considered one of the best stock PAF copies in any copy guitar; forum consensus is a pickup swap on a lower-tier model is normal and not value-destroying, but missing original Dry Z or VH-1 pickups should lower the price.

Known issues/tiering: quality tracks the original model number, not the brand — a Greco EG-500 or low LS/RLG is a plywood-or-veneer budget guitar while EG-1000/Super Real, LS-80+ and RLG-90+ are genuinely excellent; also verify country of origin since later Burny RLGs were made in Korea (much cheaper build), and early-70s Grecos can be bolt-neck with cheap hardware despite 'lawsuit era' branding.

Market/value: prices have climbed hard as 'lawsuit/MIJ' became a marketing word — good late-70s Greco EGs and 80s Tokai LS run roughly $1k–2.5k+ with top Super Real/Reborn examples higher, but forum threads (thefretboard, mylespaul) warn many NYC/online listings are 'severely overpriced' mid-tier guitars wearing lawsuit hype; the label 'lawsuit' technically applies only to pre-1978 open-book headstocks, so discount accordingly.

research: Neck feel: the Ibanez JSM (Scofield's AS200-based signature) has a flatter, more modern Ibanez feel than a Gibson — thinner shoulders and a flatter radius that 335 die-hards notice immediately; the Yamaha SA-2200 sits closer to a rounded medium C that most Gibson players adapt to instantly, and 70s Greco SAs typically have slim easy necks with low action — none of the three replicates a chunky Memphis neck, so try before assuming.

Pickups: JSM100 ships Super 58s — smooth, jazz-leaning, slightly polite versus Gibson's 57 Classics/MHS; SA-2200's stock Yamaha humbuckers are bright and articulate (forum posts on thefretboard/jazzguitar.be say it 'doesn't sound like a 335, brighter, but lovely in its own right'); 70s Greco SA pickups vary by tier (Maxon-made) and are the most commonly swapped — a swap on a Greco SA is common and mostly value-neutral, on a JSM/SA-2200 it should be disclosed and originals included.

Build vs Memphis Gibson: forum consensus (mylespaul '335 type guitar you recommend', jazzguitar.be, markweinguitarlessons comparison threads) is that JSM100 and SA-2200 fit/finish routinely beats Memphis-era Gibson — direct comparisons cite Gibsons with paint on binding, orange peel, and overspray while the Japanese builds are near-flawless; the trade-off is they are their own instruments (SA-2200 brighter, JSM darker/tighter) rather than clones of the Gibson sound.

Market/value: JSM100 and SA-2200 historically sold new at roughly 40% of a Memphis 335's price and used examples ($1.5k–2.5k) hold value well, with SA-2200 supply thin in the US (it was never widely imported) and slowly appreciating; 70s Greco SA-550/700 lawsuit-era pieces now list around $900–1,500 and are rising as the cheap alternatives dry up — resale liquidity is lower than a real Gibson, which is the main financial caveat.

Verify before buying: on a JSM confirm which model (JSM100 MIJ vs cheaper JSM10/20 lines) and check the ebony board/hardware for the signature spec; on an SA-2200 confirm MIJ serial and that it isn't the older SA-1200/2000; on Greco SA confirm tier (SA-550 is the ES-330-style full hollow, SA-700/900 the 335-style semi), check center-block presence, neck angle/heel cracks common on old MIJ semis, binding shrinkage, and whether pickups/harness are original — and on all three inspect for headstock repairs, the same as any set-neck semi.

guitars.notes: Reverb item 99761626, published 2026-07-26, offers enabled. Target R0 in ideal band; 2003 Brazilian-board run is collectible. Request nut/fret depths; verify Brazilian run via serial/COA.
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

research: Neck feel: 2015-16 True Historic R0s use the re-scanned 'True Historic' 1960 carve — slim but shouldered, roughly .82-.85" at the 1st fret, with more accurate contours than 2013-14 models; described as the most vintage-accurate slim neck of its era.
Pickups: True Historic-spec unpotted Custombuckers — sweet, open and dynamic; tonally the same league as current Custombuckers.

Known issues: MLP consensus is 2015 batches were excellent but wood/top selection slipped in 2016; double-carved tops and thin-skin lacquer check easily; correct-material TH plastics shrink and crack like the originals; 'costs 30% more for 10% better' complaints dominate period threads.

Market/value: strong collector reputation as a short-lived top-of-line run — THs resell above standard 2013-16 Historics; R0 versions are rarer than R9s and considered sleepers; beware ordinary Historics passed off as THs at TH prices.

Verify before buying: authentic TH identity (period-correct vintage-style serial starting 0 xxxx, TH-specific COA and case), finish checking/repairs under the thin lacquer, original TH plastics, and pot/solder originality.

research: Neck feel: the 2020 60th Anniversary run split 1960 production into thirds — V2 is the 'Slim C' middle-of-1960 carve (~.82"/.94-.95"), while V3 is the 'Skinny C' late-1960 profile (~.80-.81" first fret, ~.89-.90" at the 12th), described as dramatically thinner up the board — sublime for some, fatiguing for fat-neck players.
Pickups: same unpotted Alnico III Custombuckers as the core Historic line; community verdict very positive — vintage-correct output, open and dynamic.

Known issues: few model-specific faults — the usual Custom Shop lottery (nut work, occasional heavy examples, VOS finish inconsistency); some V3 buyers report neck-profile surprise; anniversary-specific parts fade unevenly on played examples.

Market/value: reasonably collectible one-year anniversary run with hand-selected specs; sells used around or slightly above standard R0 money; clean V2 examples resell more easily than V3 (very slim neck narrows the buyer pool).

Verify before buying: which neck version it actually is (get caliper measurements — V2/V3 mislabeling is common on Reverb), COA/anniversary paperwork, weight, anniversary-correct knobs/plastics, and unmodified unpotted pickups.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

guitars.note: Gibson Custom Shop 1958 Les Paul Standard Murphy Lab Ultra Light Aged Bourbon Burst (176)
research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

research: Neck feel: 1976-80 335s move to 3-piece maple necks with volute — profiles range slim to fuller medium C late in the decade; maple neck plus heavier build gives a stiffer, brighter-feeling instrument; 1977+ adds a coil-tap mini switch.

Pickups: Bill Lawrence-designed 'tarback' (epoxy-potted, ceramic) humbuckers with unusually low DCR — fans call them fat, clear 'super humbuckers'; detractors find them sterile; originals now sought-after on the parts market.
Known issues: weight is the era's defining problem — many run 8.5-10 lbs; also the volute, thick finishes, occasional sunken tops, sloppy binding/fret finishing, and commonly-swapped harnesses.
Market/value: cheapest vintage 335 window along with the early 80s — treated as gigging vintage rather than collectible; original-tarback examples have a small cult following that supports value.
Verify before buying: weight on a scale, original tarbacks (check DCR), coil-tap switch function and un-butchered wiring, neck angle/top sinking, volute-area crack repairs, finish originality.

research: Neck feel: these are not interchangeable — late-70s Greco EGs (Fujigen) typically run slim-to-medium with low comfortable setups ('plays better than Gibsons of that era' is a recurring tech comment), Tokai Love Rock LS models track 50s Gibson profiles with LS-number-dependent chunk, and Burny Super Grades are known on tokaiforum/mylespaul for deliberately fat 50s-style necks; always play or get profile measurements, model number alone doesn't tell you.

Pickups are the usual weak point and the usual swap: 70s Grecos shipped Maxon-made units (U-1000/U-2000, later the PAF-like Dry Z which is excellent and collectible), Tokai's better LS models carry respectable PAF-clones while budget LS ships duller units, Burny's VH-1 is widely considered one of the best stock PAF copies in any copy guitar; forum consensus is a pickup swap on a lower-tier model is normal and not value-destroying, but missing original Dry Z or VH-1 pickups should lower the price.

Known issues/tiering: quality tracks the original model number, not the brand — a Greco EG-500 or low LS/RLG is a plywood-or-veneer budget guitar while EG-1000/Super Real, LS-80+ and RLG-90+ are genuinely excellent; also verify country of origin since later Burny RLGs were made in Korea (much cheaper build), and early-70s Grecos can be bolt-neck with cheap hardware despite 'lawsuit era' branding.

Market/value: prices have climbed hard as 'lawsuit/MIJ' became a marketing word — good late-70s Greco EGs and 80s Tokai LS run roughly $1k–2.5k+ with top Super Real/Reborn examples higher, but forum threads (thefretboard, mylespaul) warn many NYC/online listings are 'severely overpriced' mid-tier guitars wearing lawsuit hype; the label 'lawsuit' technically applies only to pre-1978 open-book headstocks, so discount accordingly.

Verify before buying: decode the model tier and date (Greco serials/neck-pocket stamps and headstock logo style, Tokai serial + 'Love Rock' logo appears late-1980 onward, Burny serial or lack thereof — many legit early ones have no serial), check for the classic frankenguitar/parts-swap signs (mismatched pot codes, re-drilled tuner holes, replaced fingerboards), and beware Chinese counterfeits and re-decaled bodies now wearing Greco/Tokai/Burny or even Gibson logos — tokaiforum's ID threads ('Definitive Guide to Greco, Burny, Orville') are the reference for authentication.

research: Neck feel: the Ibanez JSM (Scofield's AS200-based signature) has a flatter, more modern Ibanez feel than a Gibson — thinner shoulders and a flatter radius that 335 die-hards notice immediately; the Yamaha SA-2200 sits closer to a rounded medium C that most Gibson players adapt to instantly, and 70s Greco SAs typically have slim easy necks with low action — none of the three replicates a chunky Memphis neck, so try before assuming.

Pickups: JSM100 ships Super 58s — smooth, jazz-leaning, slightly polite versus Gibson's 57 Classics/MHS; SA-2200's stock Yamaha humbuckers are bright and articulate (forum posts on thefretboard/jazzguitar.be say it 'doesn't sound like a 335, brighter, but lovely in its own right'); 70s Greco SA pickups vary by tier (Maxon-made) and are the most commonly swapped — a swap on a Greco SA is common and mostly value-neutral, on a JSM/SA-2200 it should be disclosed and originals included.

Build vs Memphis Gibson: forum consensus (mylespaul '335 type guitar you recommend', jazzguitar.be, markweinguitarlessons comparison threads) is that JSM100 and SA-2200 fit/finish routinely beats Memphis-era Gibson — direct comparisons cite Gibsons with paint on binding, orange peel, and overspray while the Japanese builds are near-flawless; the trade-off is they are their own instruments (SA-2200 brighter, JSM darker/tighter) rather than clones of the Gibson sound.

Market/value: JSM100 and SA-2200 historically sold new at roughly 40% of a Memphis 335's price and used examples ($1.5k–2.5k) hold value well, with SA-2200 supply thin in the US (it was never widely imported) and slowly appreciating; 70s Greco SA-550/700 lawsuit-era pieces now list around $900–1,500 and are rising as the cheap alternatives dry up — resale liquidity is lower than a real Gibson, which is the main financial caveat.

Verify before buying: on a JSM confirm which model (JSM100 MIJ vs cheaper JSM10/20 lines) and check the ebony board/hardware for the signature spec; on an SA-2200 confirm MIJ serial and that it isn't the older SA-1200/2000; on Greco SA confirm tier (SA-550 is the ES-330-style full hollow, SA-700/900 the 335-style semi), check center-block presence, neck angle/heel cracks common on old MIJ semis, binding shrinkage, and whether pickups/harness are original — and on all three inspect for headstock repairs, the same as any set-neck semi.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

research: Neck feel: specs say '3-piece maple neck, volute' but the range in the wild is huge — early-70s Deluxes/Customs often have slim, almost flat-shouldered necks with the small 'fretless wonder' frets on Customs (fast but hard to bend on), while late-70s/early-80s necks fill out; per mylespaul.com threads the volute is a cosmetic gripe more than a playability one, and the 3-piece maple neck is actually more break-resistant than a 1-piece mahogany Gibson neck.

Pickups: Deluxes carry Gibson mini-humbuckers — lower output, clearer and snappier than full-size 'buckers, praised in forums for cutting through a mix Tele-style; many Deluxes were routed out in the 70s/80s for full-size humbuckers (kills collector value), while Standards/Customs of the era use T-tops, now respected PAF-adjacent pickups worth real money on their own.

Known issues: weight is the big one — pancake (multi-ply) bodies 1969–77 plus maple can push Customs past 10.5–11 lbs, and weight varies wildly guitar to guitar; also watch for headstock-tip wood separation and binding chips on Customs, pancake/neck-lamination line cosmetics, and shrinking/crumbling plastics — forum consensus (e.g. mylespaul 'Pancake bodies good, bad or indifferent') is the 'Norlin era sucks' narrative is overblown, with good and bad examples every year.

Market/value: Norlins are the fastest-appreciating Gibson segment — mylespaul's 'Norlin Prices Climbing' thread and Reverb data show stock 70s Deluxes around $3.5k–4.5k and clean examples to ~$8k, Standards and Customs similar or higher, with rare finishes (cherry, sparkle, wine red) commanding premiums; 70s is 'the new vintage' as 50s/60s bursts priced everyone out.

Verify before buying: 1970–75 six-digit serials are nearly random — date via pot codes (137YYWW), 'Made in USA' stamp, volute and pancake construction details (see mylespaul FAQ 'Norlin identification 1970-1975'); check under UV/close light for headstock repairs (common, fine on a player at a discount but should knock 30-40% off), confirm mini-humbucker routes on a Deluxe are unmolested, weigh the guitar, and confirm original T-tops/mini-hums are present since pickup swaps are rampant.

research: Neck feel: the Ibanez JSM (Scofield's AS200-based signature) has a flatter, more modern Ibanez feel than a Gibson — thinner shoulders and a flatter radius that 335 die-hards notice immediately; the Yamaha SA-2200 sits closer to a rounded medium C that most Gibson players adapt to instantly, and 70s Greco SAs typically have slim easy necks with low action — none of the three replicates a chunky Memphis neck, so try before assuming.

Pickups: JSM100 ships Super 58s — smooth, jazz-leaning, slightly polite versus Gibson's 57 Classics/MHS; SA-2200's stock Yamaha humbuckers are bright and articulate (forum posts on thefretboard/jazzguitar.be say it 'doesn't sound like a 335, brighter, but lovely in its own right'); 70s Greco SA pickups vary by tier (Maxon-made) and are the most commonly swapped — a swap on a Greco SA is common and mostly value-neutral, on a JSM/SA-2200 it should be disclosed and originals included.

Build vs Memphis Gibson: forum consensus (mylespaul '335 type guitar you recommend', jazzguitar.be, markweinguitarlessons comparison threads) is that JSM100 and SA-2200 fit/finish routinely beats Memphis-era Gibson — direct comparisons cite Gibsons with paint on binding, orange peel, and overspray while the Japanese builds are near-flawless; the trade-off is they are their own instruments (SA-2200 brighter, JSM darker/tighter) rather than clones of the Gibson sound.

Market/value: JSM100 and SA-2200 historically sold new at roughly 40% of a Memphis 335's price and used examples ($1.5k–2.5k) hold value well, with SA-2200 supply thin in the US (it was never widely imported) and slowly appreciating; 70s Greco SA-550/700 lawsuit-era pieces now list around $900–1,500 and are rising as the cheap alternatives dry up — resale liquidity is lower than a real Gibson, which is the main financial caveat.

Verify before buying: on a JSM confirm which model (JSM100 MIJ vs cheaper JSM10/20 lines) and check the ebony board/hardware for the signature spec; on an SA-2200 confirm MIJ serial and that it isn't the older SA-1200/2000; on Greco SA confirm tier (SA-550 is the ES-330-style full hollow, SA-700/900 the 335-style semi), check center-block presence, neck angle/heel cracks common on old MIJ semis, binding shrinkage, and whether pickups/harness are original — and on all three inspect for headstock repairs, the same as any set-neck semi.

research: Neck feel: these are not interchangeable — late-70s Greco EGs (Fujigen) typically run slim-to-medium with low comfortable setups ('plays better than Gibsons of that era' is a recurring tech comment), Tokai Love Rock LS models track 50s Gibson profiles with LS-number-dependent chunk, and Burny Super Grades are known on tokaiforum/mylespaul for deliberately fat 50s-style necks; always play or get profile measurements, model number alone doesn't tell you.

Pickups are the usual weak point and the usual swap: 70s Grecos shipped Maxon-made units (U-1000/U-2000, later the PAF-like Dry Z which is excellent and collectible), Tokai's better LS models carry respectable PAF-clones while budget LS ships duller units, Burny's VH-1 is widely considered one of the best stock PAF copies in any copy guitar; forum consensus is a pickup swap on a lower-tier model is normal and not value-destroying, but missing original Dry Z or VH-1 pickups should lower the price.

Known issues/tiering: quality tracks the original model number, not the brand — a Greco EG-500 or low LS/RLG is a plywood-or-veneer budget guitar while EG-1000/Super Real, LS-80+ and RLG-90+ are genuinely excellent; also verify country of origin since later Burny RLGs were made in Korea (much cheaper build), and early-70s Grecos can be bolt-neck with cheap hardware despite 'lawsuit era' branding.

Market/value: prices have climbed hard as 'lawsuit/MIJ' became a marketing word — good late-70s Greco EGs and 80s Tokai LS run roughly $1k–2.5k+ with top Super Real/Reborn examples higher, but forum threads (thefretboard, mylespaul) warn many NYC/online listings are 'severely overpriced' mid-tier guitars wearing lawsuit hype; the label 'lawsuit' technically applies only to pre-1978 open-book headstocks, so discount accordingly.

Verify before buying: decode the model tier and date (Greco serials/neck-pocket stamps and headstock logo style, Tokai serial + 'Love Rock' logo appears late-1980 onward, Burny serial or lack thereof — many legit early ones have no serial), check for the classic frankenguitar/parts-swap signs (mismatched pot codes, re-drilled tuner holes, replaced fingerboards), and beware Chinese counterfeits and re-decaled bodies now wearing Greco/Tokai/Burny or even Gibson logos — tokaiforum's ID threads ('Definitive Guide to Greco, Burny, Orville') are the reference for authentication.

research: Neck feel: specs say '3-piece maple neck, volute' but the range in the wild is huge — early-70s Deluxes/Customs often have slim, almost flat-shouldered necks with the small 'fretless wonder' frets on Customs (fast but hard to bend on), while late-70s/early-80s necks fill out; per mylespaul.com threads the volute is a cosmetic gripe more than a playability one, and the 3-piece maple neck is actually more break-resistant than a 1-piece mahogany Gibson neck.

Pickups: Deluxes carry Gibson mini-humbuckers — lower output, clearer and snappier than full-size 'buckers, praised in forums for cutting through a mix Tele-style; many Deluxes were routed out in the 70s/80s for full-size humbuckers (kills collector value), while Standards/Customs of the era use T-tops, now respected PAF-adjacent pickups worth real money on their own.

Known issues: weight is the big one — pancake (multi-ply) bodies 1969–77 plus maple can push Customs past 10.5–11 lbs, and weight varies wildly guitar to guitar; also watch for headstock-tip wood separation and binding chips on Customs, pancake/neck-lamination line cosmetics, and shrinking/crumbling plastics — forum consensus (e.g. mylespaul 'Pancake bodies good, bad or indifferent') is the 'Norlin era sucks' narrative is overblown, with good and bad examples every year.

Market/value: Norlins are the fastest-appreciating Gibson segment — mylespaul's 'Norlin Prices Climbing' thread and Reverb data show stock 70s Deluxes around $3.5k–4.5k and clean examples to ~$8k, Standards and Customs similar or higher, with rare finishes (cherry, sparkle, wine red) commanding premiums; 70s is 'the new vintage' as 50s/60s bursts priced everyone out.

Verify before buying: 1970–75 six-digit serials are nearly random — date via pot codes (137YYWW), 'Made in USA' stamp, volute and pancake construction details (see mylespaul FAQ 'Norlin identification 1970-1975'); check under UV/close light for headstock repairs (common, fine on a player at a discount but should knock 30-40% off), confirm mini-humbucker routes on a Deluxe are unmolested, weigh the guitar, and confirm original T-tops/mini-hums are present since pickup swaps are rampant.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

research: Neck feel: the 2020 60th Anniversary run split 1960 production into thirds — V2 is the 'Slim C' middle-of-1960 carve (~.82"/.94-.95"), while V3 is the 'Skinny C' late-1960 profile (~.80-.81" first fret, ~.89-.90" at the 12th), described as dramatically thinner up the board — sublime for some, fatiguing for fat-neck players.
Pickups: same unpotted Alnico III Custombuckers as the core Historic line; community verdict very positive — vintage-correct output, open and dynamic.

Known issues: few model-specific faults — the usual Custom Shop lottery (nut work, occasional heavy examples, VOS finish inconsistency); some V3 buyers report neck-profile surprise; anniversary-specific parts fade unevenly on played examples.

Market/value: reasonably collectible one-year anniversary run with hand-selected specs; sells used around or slightly above standard R0 money; clean V2 examples resell more easily than V3 (very slim neck narrows the buyer pool).

Verify before buying: which neck version it actually is (get caliper measurements — V2/V3 mislabeling is common on Reverb), COA/anniversary paperwork, weight, anniversary-correct knobs/plastics, and unmodified unpotted pickups.

guitars.note: Weight exactly at 8.0 ceiling, above ideal 7.5-7.8 band. Otherwise clean all-original Memphis-built Figured with full specs disclosed.
research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

guitars.note: Gibson Custom Shop Willcutt Exclusive 1958 Les Paul Standard V2 Neck Green Lemon Fade (966)
research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

research: Neck feel: 1993-2002 Historic R0s carry an early Custom Shop interpretation of the 1960 slim taper — generally thin (~.78-.83" first fret) but less accurately carved than post-2013 reissues, with noticeable guitar-to-guitar variance; hand measurement matters more than the spec sheet.

Pickups: '57 Classics for most of the era (Burstbuckers arrive ~2001-2003) — warm, creamy, slightly compressed PAF-style; rated below Custombuckers for openness; many surviving examples have pickup swaps.

Known issues: period shortcomings vs later Historics — less accurate body carve, thick finishes on some years, incorrect plastics, no hide glue, occasional heavy bodies; otherwise solidly built (long tenon, one-piece backs); age items now: fret wear, cracked jack-area binding, shrunken plastics.

Market/value: the honest-value end of the Historic market — 'player-grade Historics' trading well below 2013+ reissues; 1999-2003 Brazilian-board examples command significant premiums; Yamano-ordered Japanese-market examples have a good selection reputation.

Verify before buying: serial decoding to confirm genuine Historic vs Classic/Standard passed off as an R0, fingerboard wood documentation on 2001-2003 claims, truss rod function, refret/repair history, originality of pickups and pots, and weight.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

guitars.model: Gibson Custom Shop 1960 Les Paul Murphy Lab Ultra Light Aged Wide Tomato Burst
guitars.pickups: Custombucker Alnico 3 (Unpotted) Pickups 2 Volume, 2 Tone, CTS 500K Audi
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

guitars.note: Memphis-era Custom Shop '63 reissue; exactly 8.0 lbs (at the hard cap). Collector-grade, no visible play wear.
research: Neck feel: the 1961 reissue's 'Skinny C' SlimTaper was scanned from originals — thin (~.80" range at the 1st fret) with vintage 1-11/16" nut; owners say convincingly close to a real early-60s slim neck, noticeably slimmer than the '59 reissue carve.

guitars.note: 2000 Gibson Custom Shop 1959 Historic Les Paul Reissue - LPR9 - Bourbon Burst - 8lbs - 6oz — *************************************************************************************************** Please Note: I Never List Anything as MINT  - See My Store F
research: Neck feel: 1993-2002 Historic R0s carry an early Custom Shop interpretation of the 1960 slim taper — generally thin (~.78-.83" first fret) but less accurately carved than post-2013 reissues, with noticeable guitar-to-guitar variance; hand measurement matters more than the spec sheet.

Pickups: '57 Classics for most of the era (Burstbuckers arrive ~2001-2003) — warm, creamy, slightly compressed PAF-style; rated below Custombuckers for openness; many surviving examples have pickup swaps.

Known issues: period shortcomings vs later Historics — less accurate body carve, thick finishes on some years, incorrect plastics, no hide glue, occasional heavy bodies; otherwise solidly built (long tenon, one-piece backs); age items now: fret wear, cracked jack-area binding, shrunken plastics.

Verify before buying: neck measurements (confirm the skinny '61 carve suits you vs the fatter '59 RI), weight, aging level and hidden damage within Murphy Lab wear, COA/case, center block rattles (tap test), original Custombuckers.

guitars.note: Tom Murphy aged (pre-Murphy Lab). No vibrato. Iced Tea is a target finish and 8.56 lb is in the ideal band, but the neck is a big one (.935/1.040) - the opposite of the V3/skinny-C preference.
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

guitars.note: Wildwood Spec 1957 Les Paul Standard - Gloss
research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

guitars.note: Near-mint Memphis Figured at 7 lbs 4.9 oz and $3,399 — lightest Memphis in the sweep, just above the 7.2 soft floor.
research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

guitars.pickups: Not stated - late-'60s ES-340 shipped with patent-number humbuckers; confirm with dealer
guitars.modifications: None - stated 100% original with original blend circuit intact
guitars.note: The only vintage example in the sweep with a published exact weight at or under the ceiling, and it lands exactly on 8.0 lbs - zero headroom. Nut measures 1.58in, the closest of any find to the buyer's ideal 1-9/16in (1.5625). NOTE ON CIRCUIT: the ES-340 has NO Varitone - it uses a master volume plus a pickup blender/phase circuit and is MONO; this one still has that original blend circuit intact (many are converted to 335 wiring). Stop bar, no Bigsby/Maestro/TP-6. Dealer dates it 1968; ES-340 production is generally 1969-1973, so verify the serial and year. Serial not published - ask. $99 US_CON shipping, offers disabled.
research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

guitars.note: Gibson Custom Shop 1958 Les Paul Standard Reissue Murphy Lab  Light Aged Lemon Burst (762)
research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Pickups: Burstbucker 61R/61T (Alnico V, slightly hot vintage-voiced) — brighter and more aggressive than Custombuckers; some find the 61T harsh into bright amps; 2019+ wiring is hand-wired with orange-drop caps, no PCB.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

guitars.note: Older listing (Jul 20) not previously captured. 7 lbs 5 oz - light, just above 7.2 soft floor. Fresh setup w/ 10s.
research: Neck feel: Memphis-era necks trend slim — 2014 dots ~.80-.88" with decent shoulder; 2015-18 add rolled fingerboard binding that owners love; profile varies by sub-model ('58/'63 reissues carry year-appropriate carves).
Pickups: MHS (Memphis Historic Spec) humbuckers — Alnico III vintage voicing; largely positive ('very vintage, mellow, smooth'), minority complaint: darker/softer than Burstbuckers into dark amps.

Known issues: QC inconsistency is the era's theme — mis-cut nuts and string-spacing errors, deep nut slots with high bridges, hide-glue squeeze-out visible through f-holes, occasional finish flaws; good examples rival Nashville CS output.

Market/value: strong used-value reputation since the Memphis plant closed (2019) — '58/'59/'63 reissues and Figured models have appreciated modestly and are the recommended sweet spot for vintage-voiced 335s under Custom Shop money.

Verify before buying: nut cut and string spacing (the era's signature flaw), setup feel or a return window, glue squeeze-out, which sub-model it actually is (big value differences), original MHS pickups, weight (7.5-9 lbs spread).

guitars.note: 1961 ES-335 Reissue - Sixties Cherry
research: Neck feel: the 1961 reissue's 'Skinny C' SlimTaper was scanned from originals — thin (~.80" range at the 1st fret) with vintage 1-11/16" nut; owners say convincingly close to a real early-60s slim neck, noticeably slimmer than the '59 reissue carve.

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers — airy PAF clarity, piano-like lows, classic 335 honk; regarded as a genuine upgrade over Memphis-era MHS/BB sets; unpotted caveat: microphonic squeal at very high gain.

Known issues: relatively few — Murphy Lab lacquer fragility/checking, weight variance (7.5-9 lbs), scattered nut/setup complaints; thin lacquer damages easily in shipping; hollow wings + unpotted pickups mean feedback management is part of ownership.

Market/value: current top-of-market for new 335s; Murphy Lab premium softens on resale (used ML often 25-30% off list) while VOS holds value best; has largely replaced clean vintage 335s in the 'best modern alternative' conversation.

Verify before buying: neck measurements (confirm the skinny '61 carve suits you vs the fatter '59 RI), weight, aging level and hidden damage within Murphy Lab wear, COA/case, center block rattles (tap test), original Custombuckers.

guitars.note: Gibson Custom Shop 1959 Les Paul Standard Reissue Sunrise Tea Burst Murphy Lab Light Aged (915)
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.

guitars.note: Gibson Custom Shop 1954 Les Paul Antique Cardinal Red Murphy Lab Ultra Light Aged
research: Neck feel: USA Standard '60s uses Gibson's modern SlimTaper — typically ~.80-.83" at the 1st fret — but forums document real unit-to-unit variance from genuinely skinny to almost medium-C; fretwork and nut quality also vary.

Known issues: weight is the big one — non-weight-relieved and commonly 9-10+ lbs (sub-9 lb examples get snapped up); also inconsistent nut slotting, occasional fret-end sprout, finish flaws under the burst.

Market/value: the mainstream benchmark Les Paul — liquid used market but steep initial depreciation (used commonly 25-35% under street); Plain Tops resell a bit lower than figured bursts; excellent players when you pick a good one.

Verify before buying: exact weight (ask for a scale photo — listings routinely guess low), neck measurements and fret ends, nut slots, top figure vs stock photos, and confirm Standard '60s vs a weight-relieved 'Classic' being misrepresented.

research: Neck feel: the Ibanez JSM (Scofield's AS200-based signature) has a flatter, more modern Ibanez feel than a Gibson — thinner shoulders and a flatter radius that 335 die-hards notice immediately; the Yamaha SA-2200 sits closer to a rounded medium C that most Gibson players adapt to instantly, and 70s Greco SAs typically have slim easy necks with low action — none of the three replicates a chunky Memphis neck, so try before assuming.

Pickups: JSM100 ships Super 58s — smooth, jazz-leaning, slightly polite versus Gibson's 57 Classics/MHS; SA-2200's stock Yamaha humbuckers are bright and articulate (forum posts on thefretboard/jazzguitar.be say it 'doesn't sound like a 335, brighter, but lovely in its own right'); 70s Greco SA pickups vary by tier (Maxon-made) and are the most commonly swapped — a swap on a Greco SA is common and mostly value-neutral, on a JSM/SA-2200 it should be disclosed and originals included.

Build vs Memphis Gibson: forum consensus (mylespaul '335 type guitar you recommend', jazzguitar.be, markweinguitarlessons comparison threads) is that JSM100 and SA-2200 fit/finish routinely beats Memphis-era Gibson — direct comparisons cite Gibsons with paint on binding, orange peel, and overspray while the Japanese builds are near-flawless; the trade-off is they are their own instruments (SA-2200 brighter, JSM darker/tighter) rather than clones of the Gibson sound.

Market/value: JSM100 and SA-2200 historically sold new at roughly 40% of a Memphis 335's price and used examples ($1.5k–2.5k) hold value well, with SA-2200 supply thin in the US (it was never widely imported) and slowly appreciating; 70s Greco SA-550/700 lawsuit-era pieces now list around $900–1,500 and are rising as the cheap alternatives dry up — resale liquidity is lower than a real Gibson, which is the main financial caveat.

Verify before buying: on a JSM confirm which model (JSM100 MIJ vs cheaper JSM10/20 lines) and check the ebony board/hardware for the signature spec; on an SA-2200 confirm MIJ serial and that it isn't the older SA-1200/2000; on Greco SA confirm tier (SA-550 is the ES-330-style full hollow, SA-700/900 the 335-style semi), check center-block presence, neck angle/heel cracks common on old MIJ semis, binding shrinkage, and whether pickups/harness are original — and on all three inspect for headstock repairs, the same as any set-neck semi.

Known issues: period shortcomings vs later Historics — less accurate body carve, thick finishes on some years, incorrect plastics, no hide glue, occasional heavy bodies; otherwise solidly built (long tenon, one-piece backs); age items now: fret wear, cracked jack-area binding, shrunken plastics.

Market/value: the honest-value end of the Historic market — 'player-grade Historics' trading well below 2013+ reissues; 1999-2003 Brazilian-board examples command significant premiums; Yamano-ordered Japanese-market examples have a good selection reputation.

Verify before buying: serial decoding to confirm genuine Historic vs Classic/Standard passed off as an R0, fingerboard wood documentation on 2001-2003 claims, truss rod function, refret/repair history, originality of pickups and pots, and weight.

research: Neck feel: these are not interchangeable — late-70s Greco EGs (Fujigen) typically run slim-to-medium with low comfortable setups ('plays better than Gibsons of that era' is a recurring tech comment), Tokai Love Rock LS models track 50s Gibson profiles with LS-number-dependent chunk, and Burny Super Grades are known on tokaiforum/mylespaul for deliberately fat 50s-style necks; always play or get profile measurements, model number alone doesn't tell you.

Pickups are the usual weak point and the usual swap: 70s Grecos shipped Maxon-made units (U-1000/U-2000, later the PAF-like Dry Z which is excellent and collectible), Tokai's better LS models carry respectable PAF-clones while budget LS ships duller units, Burny's VH-1 is widely considered one of the best stock PAF copies in any copy guitar; forum consensus is a pickup swap on a lower-tier model is normal and not value-destroying, but missing original Dry Z or VH-1 pickups should lower the price.

Known issues/tiering: quality tracks the original model number, not the brand — a Greco EG-500 or low LS/RLG is a plywood-or-veneer budget guitar while EG-1000/Super Real, LS-80+ and RLG-90+ are genuinely excellent; also verify country of origin since later Burny RLGs were made in Korea (much cheaper build), and early-70s Grecos can be bolt-neck with cheap hardware despite 'lawsuit era' branding.

Market/value: prices have climbed hard as 'lawsuit/MIJ' became a marketing word — good late-70s Greco EGs and 80s Tokai LS run roughly $1k–2.5k+ with top Super Real/Reborn examples higher, but forum threads (thefretboard, mylespaul) warn many NYC/online listings are 'severely overpriced' mid-tier guitars wearing lawsuit hype; the label 'lawsuit' technically applies only to pre-1978 open-book headstocks, so discount accordingly.

Verify before buying: decode the model tier and date (Greco serials/neck-pocket stamps and headstock logo style, Tokai serial + 'Love Rock' logo appears late-1980 onward, Burny serial or lack thereof — many legit early ones have no serial), check for the classic frankenguitar/parts-swap signs (mismatched pot codes, re-drilled tuner holes, replaced fingerboards), and beware Chinese counterfeits and re-decaled bodies now wearing Greco/Tokai/Burny or even Gibson logos — tokaiforum's ID threads ('Definitive Guide to Greco, Burny, Orville') are the reference for authentication.

research: Neck feel: 1972-75 necks are generally slim-to-medium with the Norlin headstock volute and 3-piece construction (mahogany transitioning to maple ~1975); profiles vary but rarely reach 50s chunkiness.
Pickups: T-Tops throughout — clear, tight, slightly brighter than PAFs, less midrange complexity but excellent clean and edge-of-breakup; many examples have had swaps over 50 years.

Known issues: classic Norlin gripes — weight creep on some, crooked neck sets, mediocre fretwork, sunken tops around the bridge on some examples, the volute, and hit-or-miss quality declining through the decade.

Market/value: the affordable entry into vintage 335s — early-70s examples trade far below dot-necks; 'great for the money if you play it first' consensus; clean, light, straight-necked examples appreciating modestly.

Verify before buying: neck set straightness, top sinking under the bridge, actual weight, volute-area crack/repair, T-Top originality (DCR ~7.5k), and confirm year via pot codes since Norlin serials are notoriously ambiguous.

Gibson Custom Shop 1959 Les Paul Reissue Historic Makeovers Deluxe Package 2013 - Darkburs — Here we have a cool Gibson Custom Shop ’59 Les Paul that was sent to Historic Makeovers for the Deluxe Package! It sports a Darkburst finish and has been aged t
research: Neck feel: modern core R0s ship with the '1960 V2' medium-slim carve (~.82" at the 1st fret, ~.95" at the 12th) — forum consensus calls it 'a '59 neck on a diet'; Wildwood-spec R0s also typically measure around .82" first fret, and only the V3/slim-taper variants get truly skinny (~.80"/.89").

Pickups: unpotted Custombuckers (Alnico III), widely praised on MLP/TGP as the best PAF-style pickup Gibson ships — airy, open, clear lows and classic midrange honk; Wildwood Spec versions are regarded as tonally equivalent, with differences mainly cosmetic.

Known issues: general 2019+ Historic complaints — occasional nut slot/fret-end sloppiness, inconsistent VOS/Murphy Lab finish work, weight variance (roughly 8.3-9.5 lbs, no weight relief), some checking-prone Murphy Lab lacquer; unpotted Custombuckers can squeal at high gain.

Market/value: the 2019 'reformulated' Historic line is considered the best regular-production era since True Historic; R0s trade slightly below equivalent R9s and hold value well used at roughly 60-75% of street; dealer-spec examples carry a modest resale premium.

Verify before buying: actual neck measurements (V2 vs V3 vs V1 — dealer listings are often wrong; ask for 1st/12th fret caliper numbers), weight, COA and case candy, serial format, no headstock repair under aging, and original unpotted Custombuckers.
